query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-coating tungsten regions with a thin, uniform copper layer followed by a pulsed compression plasma flow (CPF) treatment will induce rapid interfacial melting and non-equilibrium solid solution formation (W(Cu)) that minimizes void formation and phase separation, thereby enhancing thermal transport and radiation resistance while preserving mechanical durability compared to conventional copper infiltration methods.
generation.material_initial_state: Tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten regions embedded in a copper matrix produced by conventional methods (melt infiltration, spark plasma sintering, or mechanical alloying) that suffer from phase separation, poor interfacial bonding, and void formation.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin copper coating to tungsten surfaces followed by a CPF treatment with pulsed energy (around 25–35 J/cm² with pulse durations near 100 μs) to achieve rapid melting and intimate mixing at the interface.
generation.conditions: Processing in an inert atmosphere (to avoid unwanted nitride formation) with rapid cooling rates (10^6–10^7 K/s) typical of CPF, applied to fusion-reactor joint components under high thermal loads and irradiation conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a non-equilibrium W(Cu) solid solution and a finely dispersed intergranular structure that promotes continuous contact with minimal voids.
generation.mechanism: The copper coating melts and mixes at the tungsten interface under the intense, pulsed plasma impact; subsequent rapid cooling freezes in a homogeneous, defect-minimized structure that provides superior thermal pathways and resistance to irradiation-induced damage.
generation.predicted_outcome: A W–Cu composite with enhanced thermal conductivity and radiation tolerance, exhibiting fewer voids and improved interfacial strength compared to components fabricated via conventional molten copper filling or powder-based methods.
generation.baseline: Standard techniques (e.g., molten copper infiltration, spark plasma sintering, or mechanical alloying) that typically yield composites with voids, phase separation, and defects deleterious to thermal and mechanical performance under irradiation.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective for fusion-reactor heat sink components where the operational temperatures remain below copper’s boiling point and the irradiation environment mimics conditions encountered in current fusion reactor designs.
generation.uncertainty: While the CPF-treated composite is predicted to show improved thermal transport and durability, the exact quantitative enhancements and long-term behavior under cyclic thermal and irradiation loads remain to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one using the proposed method (copper pre-coating plus CPF treatment) and one using a conventional copper infiltration or powder-sintering process. Subject both to simulated fusion conditions including high thermal flux and helium ion irradiation. Perform comparative microstructural (SEM/TEM), thermal (non-contact thermal diffusivity), and mechanical (tensile, shear, and hardness) analyses.
measurements: Mechanical testing under simulated irradiation conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the CPF-treated composite does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least 20% higher thermal conductivity or a notably lower void density, coupled with maintained or superior mechanical properties under irradiation) in comparison to the conventional process baseline.

cited_evidence.text: The development and construction of thermonuclear (fusion) reactors are essential to the world’s energy system. One of the main persistent problems in fusion reactor construction is the selection of materials for plasma-facing components []. The materials must have high sputtering resistance, high melting point, low deuterium/tritium retention, high thermal conductivity, and superior mechanical properties. Tungsten is considered the main promising candidate for this role []. For example, the ITER program has been conducting research on tungsten-based first-wall components. On the other hand, copper is a promising material for heat sinks due to its high thermal conductivity. The tungsten monoblocks in the first wall and copper sinks must connect with the interlayer providing high thermal conductivity and low mechanical stress. Therefore, tungsten-copper alloys can be an effective solution to the interface problem [].

Overall, the work demonstrated the fundamental opportunity of creating alloys based on tungsten and copper by successively applying copper coating to the tungsten surface and using pulsed action of compression plasma flows with a pulse duration of 100 μs, with an absorbed energy density of 35–55 J/cm2. The results demonstrate the formation of a composite structure based on individual phases of tungsten and copper, and due to the high-speed crystallization of the molten surface layer, a solid solution of W(Cu) with a distorted crystal lattice is formed. Analysis of radiation effects during irradiation of tungsten and tungsten-copper alloy samples with helium ions with an energy of 40 keV and doses of (1–3) × 1017 cm−2 showed that tungsten samples pre-treated with CPF in the melting and mixing mode of the near-surface layer have increased radiation resistance. In the near-surface region, corresponding to the helium ion range, there is a distortion of the tungsten phase crystal lattice, which causes mechanical destruction of the surface.
